extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational humor, NLP, and interpretable machine learning
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating computational systems that detect humor by grounding features and classifiers in existing humor theories, with an emphasis on interpretability and quantitative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-driven grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational approaches to detecting humor should be based on existing humor theories rather than purely data-driven heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes bridging the gap between humor theory research and computational detection by creating an interpretable framework grounded in multiple humor theories (THInC). Systems should explicitly represent theoretical constructs so that model behavior can be related back to established theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretable model architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interpretable classifiers (e.g., GA2M) such that the model's decisions and feature contributions are transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: THInC ensembles interpretable GA2M classifiers, each representing a different humor theory. Emphasis is on associative interpretability that enables analysis of proxy efficacy and alignment of joke features with theories. Prefer model choices that support inspection and explanation of feature effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proxy features reflecting theory aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineered proxy features should quantitatively reflect different aspects of humor theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework engineers a transparent flow to actively create proxy features that map onto theory-derived constructs. Feature design should be explicit about which theoretical aspect it operationalizes, enabling quantitative measurement of that aspect's contribution to humor detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble of theory-specific classifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent different humor theories with separate classifiers and combine them (ensemble) to capture multiple theoretical perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each GA2M classifier in the ensemble corresponds to a different humor theory; ensembling allows integrating complementary signals from multiple theories and preserves interpretability at the theory level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard evaluation metrics (performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate detection systems with standard classification metrics such as F1 score; reported implementation achieves an F1 of 0.85.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use balanced, interpretable metrics (precision, recall, F1) to report performance. Performance targets should be reported alongside interpretability analyses to demonstrate both efficacy and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of features with theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze and report how engineered features align with the theoretical constructs they are intended to represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The associative interpretability of the framework enables analysis of proxy efficacy and alignment of joke features with theories. Practitioners should document which features map to which theoretical aspects and assess that mapping's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of globally contributing features
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and report features that globally contribute to humor classification across models/theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the interpretability properties of chosen models to surface globally important features and discuss their roles. This helps understand common signals of humor irrespective of theoretical framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative comparison of humor theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide mechanisms to compare humor theories automatically and quantitatively using model-level and feature-level analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework is presented as a first step in automatically comparing humor theories in a quantitative manner. Systems should enable comparisons (e.g., via separate theory-aligned classifiers, feature importances, or performance contributions) to assess which theories better explain observed humorous content.
